title: From C Source to Executable: Preprocessing, Compilation, Assembly and Linking
learningObjectives: Describe the major stages that transform C source files into an executable program.
Distinguish preprocessing, compilation, assembly and linking, including the role of headers and object files.
Explain the difference between a compile-time diagnostic, a linker error and a run-time failure.
Use compiler commands to build a C program and inspect intermediate outputs when supported.
Recognize that toolchain stages and options vary by compiler and target platform.

understand.concept: A C build transforms source code into a program through several toolchain stages. Preprocessing handles directives such as #include and macros. The compiler translates the preprocessed translation unit. An assembler may produce an object file containing machine code and metadata. The linker combines object files and required libraries, resolves external references and creates an executable or another target artifact. Toolchains may combine or reorganize these stages, but understanding their responsibilities makes build failures easier to diagnose.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding Compile, link and run: source, preprocessing, object files, linking and executable helps you reason about program behaviour instead of memorizing syntax. It is useful in exams, debugging and building reliable C applications.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a tool with a precise contract: it has valid inputs, defined operations and observable results.
understand.analogyLimit: An analogy is only an aid; the C standard and the relevant function specifications determine actual behaviour.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Source code is not the executable

A file such as main.c contains C source code. A compiler toolchain transforms it into a target-specific program.

## 2. Preprocessing

The preprocessor handles directives beginning with #. For example, #include <stdio.h> makes declarations from the standard I/O header available to the translation unit. Macro expansion and conditional compilation also occur here. Preprocessing does not itself produce the final machine-code program.

## 3. Compilation and assembly

The compiler checks the translation unit against C language rules and translates it for the selected target. A toolchain may produce assembly text as an intermediate output. An assembler converts assembly instructions into an object file.

## 4. Linking

The linker combines object files and libraries, resolves external references and produces the requested output. If a called function has no matching definition or library implementation, the build may fail during linking rather than during C syntax checking.

## 5. Build and inspect

With GCC, a common command is: gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 main.c -o app. The -E option requests preprocessing only, -S requests assembly output, and -c requests an object file without linking. Exact options and output conventions can vary by toolchain.

## 6. Diagnose the stage

A preprocessing error may involve a missing header or invalid directive. A compiler diagnostic may identify invalid syntax or a type constraint violation. A linker error may report an unresolved external symbol or duplicate definition. A run-time failure occurs after a program has been built and started.

A successful build proves only that the toolchain produced the requested artifact. It does not prove that the program's logic is correct or safe. Test expected, boundary and invalid inputs.

examples.title: Build a single source file
examples.explanation: Save as main.c and build with gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 main.c -o app. The compiler driver coordinates the required toolchain stages.

examples.title: Inspect separate toolchain outputs
examples.code:
gcc -E main.c -o main.i
gcc -S main.i -o main.s
gcc -c main.s -o main.o
gcc main.o -o app
examples.explanation: This illustrates preprocessing, assembly generation, object-file creation and linking as separate steps. Real compiler drivers may perform additional work, and exact commands can vary by platform.

practise.guidedTask: Build a small C program with warnings enabled. Use documented compiler options to inspect preprocessed output and, if supported, an assembly file and object file. Record which stage creates each artifact, then link and run the program.
practise.independentTask: Create two source files where one defines a function and the other calls it. Compile each to an object file, link them, then temporarily remove the function definition and observe the linker diagnostic. Restore it and test the executable.
hints: The compiler driver often coordinates several separate tools.
Preprocessing output is not yet a final executable.
An object file can contain unresolved external references.
A linker error is different from a C syntax error.
A successful link does not prove run-time correctness.

questions.prompt: Which stage expands directives such as #include and #define?
questions.explanation: Preprocessing handles source directives and macro expansion before the main translation stage.

questions.prompt: What is a typical object file used for?
options: It contains compiled code and metadata that can be linked with other objects
It is always the final executable
questions.answer: It contains compiled code and metadata that can be linked with other objects
questions.explanation: Object files are inputs to the linker and may contain unresolved external references.

questions.prompt: An object file refers to a function whose definition is missing. At which stage is this commonly reported?
questions.explanation: The linker resolves references between object files and libraries.

questions.prompt: What does GCC's -c option commonly request?
options: Produce an object file without linking
questions.answer: Produce an object file without linking
questions.explanation: The -c option stops before the linking stage.

questions.prompt: A program builds successfully. What does that prove?
options: The toolchain produced the requested build artifact, not that the program is logically correct
questions.answer: The toolchain produced the requested build artifact, not that the program is logically correct
questions.explanation: Testing and review are still required after a successful build.
